en: Raised a clamor from the earth;
Upon every mountaintop,
Radiance poured as the sun rose.
From the palace in the tower,
Holding a golden staff,
Waving her white kerchief,
Wrapped in a loose fur coat,
The unfortunate woman walked with measured grace,
Imploring the Creator.
Within the tower with its threshold,
The helpless, ill-fated woman
Stood in true labor.
Mountainous Kyyaz now saw
Your sister-in-law’s travail.
Seeing it, brave Kyyaz
Prepared himself like a hawk;
An idea from the unseen
Came to brave Kyyaz.
Rumbling in fury,
He addressed the great dark host of the Jediger:
“Assemble before the khan!”
Khan Kyyaz began to rage.
When they saw Khan Kyyaz’s wrath,
The Jediger acted as though an enemy had come;
Crying, “May our people’s road be fortunate!”
They scattered in fright.
The tower was the emblem of the khan—
Ask no more about that tower:
Its full height was magnificent.
Seeing him would set the heart at ease,
Saying, “A son born of a khan,”
Looking upon him would satisfy my blood,
We have made him our ward and have no regrets.
If he matures into a hero,
If he becomes the equal of heroic sons,
We shall give him the throne and make him khan,
And make him a worthy hero,
We shall take shelter in him
When this child grows up.
He will reach Afghanistan and lay it waste;
How could Jet-Kait escape unharmed?
They will don armor no arrow can pierce,
And attack a people
No man has heard of or seen.
They will journey to lands
No ear has heard of and no nation has seen.
If your child survives,
Firwood spears will clash,
And wherever he strikes, war will rage.
If your son lives,
The Jediger of Jeti-Özön
Will reach the foe and feast on spoils.
Across the face of the earth
He will be famed as Kyyaz’s son.
Our dream has turned out well:
The captive woman will bear a son,
And our cause will not fare badly.
The child this woman bears you
Will have perfect fortune;
The enemy who challenges him will be humbled.
His gaze will be a surging flood;
Whoever grapples with him will be humbled.
The way he faces will blaze like fire;
The enemy will halt without confronting him.
He will be a flame burning on the mountain pass;
Without confronting him, the enemy
Will halt!
If your child survives,
See what his valor will be:
In the marshes of Chogulma
They had gathered together.
They recorded the days,
Saying, “This is the count of days,”
And vied in calculation.
They recorded the months,
Saying, “This is the count of months,”
And disputed among themselves.
They reckoned the count of days
And entered the days in writing.
They reckoned the count of months
And learned the truth for certain.
Speaking softly but firmly,
Bearded hero Kutu
Began to address brave Kyyaz:
“When we count the months,
A full twelve months have passed;
The child the woman is to bear
Is truly your own child.
When the woman gives birth,
Slaughter ninety beasts for the feast
And give the child a fitting name.
Let your heart know no doubt:
Truly, the child sprung from your loins
Is your own.
If it is a son,
Choose the finest of all names.
Saying, ‘Kyyaz has gained a child,’
Wash away every last sorrow
From your heart.
If a fierce enemy host should come,
We shall set him against them,
And make him our war club.
We shall make him master among the people,
A giant among the Jediger nation,
And take him as our champion ram.
If his daily fortunes prosper
And he grows greater day by day,
Like that towering mountain,
We shall make him our mighty bulwark.
Saying, ‘Now he has come of age,’
Heed these words.
If a son is born, Jediger,
Slaughter countless beasts for his feast,
And put aside all such
Slurred and foolish talk.
Let us strike down whoever goes astray;
So none may babble slander,
My people, let us lick
The edge of the sword!”
They kissed the bullets and swore an oath.
When the Jediger heard this, they said:
“Enough, warrior Kutu,
What you say is sound counsel.
May the seven forefathers of anyone
Who disobeys you be infidels.
Do not babble, Jediger;
Our father Kutu’s words
Are wisdom.”
All manner of men live among a people;
If someone should suddenly babble,
Or rave without warning,
Let us beat him to pieces
And punish him cruelly.
Let us ignore his pleas
And gouge out his eyes in punishment.
Let us raid his mares from the pasture;
One who spreads such idle talk
May well have his wrath aroused.”
The Jediger shouted and the people stirred,
And they sealed their pledge.
After Kutu had spoken these words,
The Jediger dispersed.
The people departed one by one,
And the Jediger rode away.
While matters stood thus among the Jediger,
The Jediger’s brave Kyyaz
Was an extraordinary champion,
Yet Kyyaz’s treachery
Was as vast as Ala-Too.
He would weary those who fought him
And make those who grappled with him crawl.
He would bewilder whoever met him
And straighten whoever opposed him.
No man could face him.
If this son of yours survives,
He will ride along the Sombuk River,
And the man who contests him will crawl.
He will meet anyone who challenges him;
If your son matures into a champion,
Whoever clashes with him will crawl.
If he turns, strife will begin;
Many who see him
Will break ranks and flee.
When the child is old enough to play,
Let us hang a sword from his neck.
Let no winged creature strike him,
No beaked creature peck him;
Let him drink from no dirty vessel
And wear no soiled clothing.
Saying, “He is heroic Kyyaz’s son,
Himself a manifest hero,”
Let us cherish him as our protector.
If by chance she bears a son,
Whoever says this or that,
Whoever feeds on filthy gossip,
Let us cut off his head with a sword
And utterly destroy
Every scrap of his property!
If someone suddenly babbles,
If the people should rave without warning,
Brand him a corrupter of the nation
And give him that name.
If there is some prattling wretch,
Seize him and gouge out his eyes.
Let us plunder much from him
And levy a heavy fine;
If some fool raves,
Drag him along the road
And hand him over to the executioners.
He had brought them before him,
And drawn them close to his side.
Speaking softly but firmly,
Champion Kyyaz began:
“There are seven chambers in the treasury.”
The Jediger’s brave Kyyaz
Opened the treasury doors.
Heavy bolts of silk brocade
And all manner of coins he lavishly
Scattered among the old women,
Yielding to their demands.
Bright gold and white silver—
Without making them ask, brave Kyyaz
Gave the accursed old women
Sacks filled with treasure.
What else could wretched Kyyaz do?
He did not cease his villainy:
He smeared poison on their edges
And prepared seven razors.
On each razor’s edge
Was poison fatal at a touch.
“If Aichürök bears a girl,
Wrap her in pure white,
And saying, ‘My khan, your wish is granted,’
Bring me the glad tidings!
It was a girl I desired;
If you fulfill my desire,
By your fathers’ graves, seven mothers,
I will grant whatever you ask.
If you truly believe my words
And truly serve me,
But she bears a son,
He will fall into servitude in the end,
And ultimately harbor an enemy’s hatred.
In the end he will do no good,
But bear immeasurable enmity.
If she bears a son,
Cut his umbilical cord with it,” he said.
The “razor steeped in poison”
Was given to the brood of the accursed,
The seven sorcerous old women.
Such was the nature of those crones:
They had reached ninety without dying,
And never suffered earthly torment.
They were witches like ogres,
And their people followed them into wickedness.
At the hands of the seven old women,
Many infants who might have grown
And come to be called children
Had died and vanished.
They were drunkards who meddled in disputes,
Greedy schemers who plundered the world.
The seven sorcerous old women
Were never satisfied, even in death;
Even with their heads beneath the earth,
They would not cease corrupting the people.
At every step they plotted,
And never abandoned their great wickedness.
People trembled at the sight of them;
Great spell-casters and enchanters,
All seven were nothing but calamity,
Practiced in uncanny arts.
They were the very eyes of seven corrupters,
Calamity itself.
Each was a true scourge.
Whenever a woman went into labor,
They would blindfold her,
